Subject: Measurement question on committed tokens + streaming

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for the demo last week — James and I reviewed the latency numbers and the proposed committed token tiers in the pricing sheet. Before we surface this to procurement I need one clarification on how committed tokens are measured against our real workload: we have many user sessions that keep a 60k token context (search+web-history) and then stream short completions (50-300 tokens) back to the user many times during the session.

Two specific asks:
- When we say "committed tokens/month", are we billed on the entire context length included with each request (the 60k prefix) or is the platform charging only for the delta (the newly generated tokens) if we enable prefix/KV caching?
- For streaming responses that are kept open and emit many small deltas, is there any per-call minimum or rounding that could cause small bursts to be billed inefficiently? Example: 40 streams x 120 tokens = 4,800 tokens — but if there's a per-stream floor that rounds to 1,000 tokens, that blows our math.

We're trying to map committed tiers to expected spend; the attached usage sample shows our composition. Can you confirm?

Thanks,
Sophie

Hi Sophie — great questions, thanks for the detail and for attaching the sample. Short answer up front so you can pass to procurement quickly: committed-token usage counts the tokens that traverse our metering window; with KV/prefix caching enabled we do not re-bill the full 60k prefix on every request, only the tokens that are new or that miss cache. There are two important caveats I'll summarize below.

Important caveats / mechanics:
- Per-request metering: Redwood meters at the request level (prompt + generated tokens). If you send the full 60k context every time and caching is disabled, that context will count on each request. If you enable KV/prefix caching for that session, cached prefixes are not recharged token-for-token on cache hits — we bill only the regenerated tokens plus a small cache-miss fraction when we refresh segments.
- Aggregation window: For committed tiers we apply a 1-hour aggregation window for conversational sessions (to allow many small streams to aggregate). That means many short streaming deltas from the same session within the window can be rolled together for metering purposes for billing optimization (reduces rounding waste).
- Rounding quantum: Metering rounds to a 32-token quantum for per-request accounting; however, after aggregation the effective rounding loss is amortized across the whole window. So 40 streams x 120 tokens shouldn't be rounded to 40 * 32 in committed calculations if they fall into the same aggregation window and are from the same session.

We'll review your specific sample and confirm exact numbers; I'm looping in Marissa and Vivek to validate the SOW pricing lines.

Next steps: I'll get back with a worked example from your sample and an updated pricing sheet that shows committed spend vs. best-effort per-token billing.

Best,
Tessa

Sophie — copied the math below based on the Usage_Sample_Jan you shared. I kept it conservative and called out cache-miss assumptions.

Example (conservative):
- Session prefix: 60,000 tokens (cached once at session start)
- Average stream delta: 120 generated tokens, 40 streams in the hour = 4,800 generated tokens
- Cache miss rate assumed: 5% (some segments refresh) => extra ~3,000 tokens billed across the hour for prefix refreshes (not 60k each time)
- Metering quantum: 32-token rounding per request, but with 1-hour aggregation the 40 streams get merged for committed accounting; effective rounding cost < 2% in this example.

Conclusion: with KV/prefix caching + 1-hour aggregation you should see committed billing that closely tracks the generated deltas (so roughly ~7–8k tokens for the hour in the conservative scenario), not 40 * 60k.

Marissa — for SOW we offer two conservative options: (A) committed monthly tokens that are measured post-aggregation (recommended for Greenfield), or (B) pay-as-you-go with a committed discount band applied to all tokens (simpler but less predictable). Sophie — I'll attach the worked spreadsheet in the next email.

One additional nuance: a subset of our product emits ephemeral debug streams (very chatty) tied to a session ID but with different correlation keys; they originate from the same session but we rotate session IDs every 20 minutes for privacy. Will those still coalesce into the 1-hour aggregation or will rotation break the window and cause re-billing of prefixes?

Also procurement asks whether you can cap rounding exposure for the first 3 months of the SOW while we ramp. They want to see an upper bound on wasted rounding in case our production behavior differs from the sample.

Sophie

Subject: Re: Measurement question on committed tokens + streaming

Sophie — quick answers:
- Session rotation: by default aggregation is keyed by persistent session identifier. If you rotate session IDs every 20 minutes that will break aggregation; however, we can enable cross-session affinity for a named workspace or user ID so related sessions coalesce into the same billing window. That is a configuration toggle (we've done it for a couple of privacy-conscious customers) and we can include it in the SOW.
- Rounding cap: we can offer a 3-month protection addendum: if your rounding/aggregation waste for the first billing quarter exceeds 6% of committed spend, we'll credit the excess back (applies only to the committed tiers in SOW option A). We usually reserve this for enterprise deals where the customer has a ramp profile; happy to include it as a negotiation point.

I've attached an updated SOW that spells the aggregation/keying behavior and the proposed rounding cap. Sophie — if this looks good, Tessa can route the SOW for signature and we can push a DocuSign link.

-Marissa
